READING THE RIVER · ARTICLE

Where Gold Settles in a River—and How to Test Your Hunch

By the Old-Timer · Published October 7, 2026

The Old-Timer is Gold Trails’ editorial voice. Content assembled with assistance from ChatGPT. Sources are linked throughout.

A promising river spot is a question you can test. Start with evidence that the drainage carries gold, look for places where sediment has been sorted or trapped, and compare small samples before committing your afternoon to one hole. A handsome bend alone cannot tell you what is in the gravel.

Before you get your boots muddy

  • Look for a gold-bearing drainage before choosing a particular crack or bar.
  • Use river features to choose samples, not to promise a find.
  • Compare similar amounts of material and record exactly where each came from.
  • Repeat a promising result; one flake is a clue, not a measured deposit.

First, does this river have a gold story?Link

Placer gold comes from the breakdown and redistribution of gold-bearing material. USGS distinguishes these sediment concentrations from gold still held in its original rock. Your first useful research is therefore about the drainage: documented occurrences, local geology, and historical workings. These can help establish a reason to sample; an old mine on a map is not proof that your chosen bar contains recoverable gold. GoldU.S. Geological SurveyLode and placer depositsExplains placer formation, gold near bedrock, and heavy-mineral concentrates.View original source ↗Opens another website in a new tab; this article stays open..

Write down what you know and what you are guessing. “Gold documented upstream” and “this bend looks good” belong in different columns of your notebook. That small distinction keeps enthusiasm from turning into evidence.

The river sorts material over timeLink

Water does more than carry a few flakes downstream. It moves sediment, rearranges the bed, and leaves deposits that later flows may disturb again. USGS explains that gold can concentrate near bedrock as high water agitates the moving bed material and gold works downward. Today’s quiet surface is only one moment in that longer history. GoldU.S. Geological SurveyLode and placer depositsExplains placer formation, gold near bedrock, and heavy-mineral concentrates.View original source ↗Opens another website in a new tab; this article stays open..

Two water terms help keep observations honest. Discharge is the volume passing a point per unit time. Velocity describes water movement at a location. A gauge reading for the river does not tell you the speed in a particular pocket. Likewise, bed load moves on or near the bottom, while suspended sediment travels in the water column. Three kinds of places worth testingLink

The Forest Service and BLM’s Kenai gold-panning guide identifies inside bends, point-bar heads, downstream sides of boulders, and bedrock pockets as candidate sites. Treat these as suggestions for sampling, not universal rules. Gold Panning · 2018 revisionU.S. Forest Service & BLMPrinted page 8 · PDF page 12Identifies candidate sampling locations and bedrock or clay concentration.View original source ↗Opens another website in a new tab; this article stays open..

Inside bends and bars

A bend gives you several possible sampling positions. Label them separately rather than mixing everything into a single pan. If you combine the samples immediately, you lose the ability to learn which position supplied the gold.

Accessible bedrock cracks

Crevices can retain gold-bearing sediment. The guide also describes gold reaching bedrock or an impermeable clay layer. Keep different layers separate in your notes; a compact surface is not automatically solid rock. Gold Panning · 2018 revisionU.S. Forest Service & BLMPrinted page 8 · PDF page 12Identifies candidate sampling locations and bedrock or clay concentration.View original source ↗Opens another website in a new tab; this article stays open..

Deposits beside obstructions

A boulder changes nearby flow, but “behind a rock” is not a complete sample description. Record which side, how far away, and what layer you sampled. Do not undermine or move unstable boulders to chase a theory.

A feature helps you choose where to investigate. A sample tells you what that particular material yielded. Neither tells you, by itself, what the next bucket will contain.

A small, repeatable sampling routineLink

Here is a suggested Gold Trails notebook routine, rather than a formal mineral-resource assessment. Its purpose is to make your next decision less dependent on memory.

  1. Choose a few accessible positions. Give each a label, such as A, B, and C. Note the feature and layer before disturbing it.
  2. Use a consistent starting measure. A marked scoop or container helps. Record whether the volume is before or after classification, and keep that choice consistent.
  3. Keep the processing comparable. Use the same classifier and panning approach. If you spill material or rush a pan, mark the result as uncertain.
  4. Record what you actually recover. Note visible gold, approximate particle sizes, and anything that made identification uncertain. Photograph the result if useful.
  5. Repeat the more promising position. Keep the repeat sample separate. Agreement is more useful than one exciting pan.
  6. Decide what the evidence supports. Continue testing, shift position, or move on. A weak result is useful information too.

A useful entry might read: “B2; exposed gravel beside bedrock; one measured scoop before screening; same screen as B1; two tiny suspected flakes; identification needs checking.” This is a fictional notebook example, not a reported field result.

What a pan can—and cannot—tell youLink

Counting visible particles can help organize observations, but a particle count is not the same as gold mass. Ten tiny flakes and one larger piece cannot be ranked by counting alone. Nor does a single sample establish the average grade of a bar.

Black sand is another clue with limits. USGS describes magnetite and other heavy minerals occurring in these concentrates. Finding them does not establish the amount of gold present. Record the observation without promoting it into a guarantee. GoldU.S. Geological SurveyLode and placer depositsExplains placer formation, gold near bedrock, and heavy-mineral concentrates.View original source ↗Opens another website in a new tab; this article stays open..

Be equally careful with a disappointing pan. It describes that sample and your recovery from it. Before drawing a broad conclusion, ask whether your sample position, material volume, or technique changed. The goal is a fair comparison, not an argument with the river.

Your before-you-dig checklistLink

  • Confirm current access, claim status, and permitted methods with the relevant land manager. A promising geological location is not permission to prospect.
  • Stay with safely accessible material. A sample is never worth entering dangerous current or cold water.
  • Avoid undercutting banks and disturbing vegetation. Follow local restoration and habitat requirements.
  • Bring a notebook, a consistent sampling measure, and a way to keep samples separate.

BLM distinguishes low-disturbance hand panning from activities that require additional review under its surface-management framework. Rules depend on the place and activity; check the current local requirements. The satisfying part is learning to ask a better question with each pan. Find a reason to look, make a comparison you can trust, and let the result guide the next small step.
